Condition: VARY

## Sample kind

- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The Weight of Unsent Letters

I keep a drawer for letters I never sent. Not the romantic kind, though there are a few of those too, curled in their envelopes like sleeping cats. Mostly they're to people who are still alive, people I see regularly, people who would probably be confused if they received them. A letter to my mother explaining why I don't call enough. A letter to my college roommate apologizing for the night I came home drunk and said something cruel about his girlfriend. A letter to my boss, which I wrote during a particularly bad week, that begins "I have reached the end of what I can pretend."

The drawer is oak, inherited from my grandmother, and it smells like cedar and old paper. I open it maybe twice a year. I read one letter, sometimes two, then close it again. The letters don't change. They accumulate like sediment, layer upon layer of things I needed to say but couldn't, in the moment, face-to-face.

I think about this sometimes when I'm at parties, making small talk, laughing at jokes I don't find funny. There's a version of me that exists in these letters. She's more honest. She's also more alone. She says things like "I am afraid I am becoming someone I don't recognize" and "I don't know how to be loved" and "I think I need help but I don't know how to ask for it."

The me at parties says "I'm fine, thanks, just busy with work." Both are true. Both are incomplete. The question is which incompleteness I can live with.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Not every night, but often enough that I've started to think of it as a kind of clock, a reminder that the world continues its indifferent rotation. I used to get angry. Now I find it almost comforting, this proof that something else is awake, something else is struggling with the dark.

I have trouble sleeping. It's not insomnia exactly—I sleep, eventually, deeply, the kind of sleep that leaves you drooling on your pillow—but the getting there is a negotiation. My mind wants to review the day, rehearse conversations, compose emails I'll never send. It wants to solve problems that don't exist yet. It wants to be anywhere but here, in this bed, in this body, in this particular moment that will never come again.

I've tried everything. White noise. Meditation apps with soothing voices. Reading until my eyes burn. Counting sheep, which I've always found absurd—why sheep? Why not, I don't know, tax forms? Something actually boring. Last week I tried counting backwards from 1000 in French, which I studied in high school and have mostly forgotten. *Mille, neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf, neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-huit...* I made it to about 850 before my mind wandered to whether the French actually count down differently, whether there's some cultural reason for the awkwardness of *quatre-vingt-dix-neuf*, and then I was thinking about my high school French teacher, Mrs. Patterson, who wore too much perfume and once cried in class when she talked about her divorce, and then I was awake again, fully, staring at the ceiling.

---

There's a photograph of me at seven that I can't look at without feeling something I don't have a name for. I'm standing in front of a birthday cake, mouth open in that particular way children have, half-laugh, half-scream, the candle smoke still curling upward. My eyes are bright. I look, in that photograph, like someone who believes that good things will keep happening, that the world is fundamentally generous, that love is simple and available and enough.

I don't know when that changed. I don't know if it changed gradually, like erosion, or all at once, like a door closing. I know that I spent years trying to get back to that girl, as if she were a place I could return to, a version of myself I could resurrect through effort and intention. I don't think she's coming back. I think she was a kind of grace, temporary, given to children so they can survive the knowledge of what's coming.

But I keep the photograph. I keep it in the same drawer as the letters, though it's not a letter. It's a question, really. *Who were you? What did you know that I've forgotten?*

---

I went to the doctor last month for a physical. Everything was fine, the doctor said. Blood pressure good, cholesterol good, "you're in great shape for someone your age." I'm thirty-four. I don't know what that means, great shape for thirty-four. I wanted to ask if he meant I was doing well compared to other thirty-four-year-olds, or if he was surprised I wasn't falling apart, or if he was just being polite. I didn't ask. I said thank you and scheduled my next appointment and left.

In the parking lot I sat in my car for ten minutes. I wasn't crying. I wasn't anything, really. Just sitting. The doctor had been kind, efficient, forgettable. He would not remember me tomorrow. This is the arrangement we've made, this transaction of care: I pay, he examines, we both pretend it matters more than it does. I don't blame him. I don't blame me. But I felt, sitting there, the particular loneliness of being known by no one, of being a body that functions, a set of numbers on a chart, a brief entry in a database that will eventually be deleted.

I drove home. I made dinner. I watched a show I didn't really follow. I went to bed.

---

My mother calls on Sundays. We talk about the weather, about my sister's new job, about whether I've eaten enough vegetables. She asks if I'm dating anyone. I say no, not seriously, and she says well, you're still young, you have time, and I say yes, I know, I have time, and we both know that time is not the issue, that the issue is something else, something we don't have words for, something that lives in the pauses between her questions and my answers.

I love her. I don't know how to tell her. I don't know if she knows. I think about the letter in my drawer, the one that begins "I don't call enough because—" and I can't finish it. I can't finish it because I don't know what comes after the because. Because I'm afraid? Because I'm ashamed? Because I don't know how to be the person she wants me to be, the person I was supposed to become, the son who calls more, who visits more, who is more grateful, more present, more *there*?

She's getting older. I can see it, the way she moves, the way she forgets words sometimes, mid-sentence, and has to start over. I want to tell her things. I want to tell her that I think about her constantly, that I carry her with me, that she is the reason I am who I am, for better and worse. I want to tell her that I am afraid, that I am lonely, that I don't know how to live the life I have. I want to tell her that I love her, that I have always loved her, that the not-calling is not a measure of that love, that it's something else, something broken in me, something I'm trying to fix.

Instead I say "I'm fine, Mom, how are you?" and she says "I'm good, I'm good, just busy" and we talk about the weather some more.

---

There's a man I see at the coffee shop. I don't know his name. I've never spoken to him. He comes in around 7:30, orders a black coffee, sits in the corner with a book. He's maybe sixty, with a beard that's gone mostly gray, and glasses that he keeps pushing up his nose. He reads for an hour, maybe two, then leaves. I've started timing my own arrival to overlap with his, though I would never admit this, even to myself, quite so baldly.

I don't want to be his friend. I don't want to know his story. I want, I think, to see someone else being alone in a way that looks peaceful, that looks chosen. He doesn't look at his phone. He doesn't look around the room, waiting, hoping. He just reads, and drinks his coffee, and exists in a way that seems complete unto himself.

I've started bringing my own book, though I don't read it. I sit near him, close enough to see the titles, far enough to seem uninterested. *The Brothers Karamazov*. *Austerlitz*. *The Overstory*. Books I've read, mostly, or started, or bought and abandoned. I pretend to read. I watch him, out of the corner of my eye, and I try to learn something. I try to learn how to be alone without it being a failure, a waiting, a gap to be filled.

He never looks at me. This is probably for the best. If he did, if he smiled, if he said hello, I don't know what I would do. I think I would panic. I think I would leave and not come back, because the spell would be broken, because he would become a person instead of a lesson, and I don't know how to be a person around other people.

---

I went to my father's funeral last year. I don't talk about this much. There's a version of me that existed before, and a version that exists after, and they don't quite connect. The funeral was small. He'd outlived most of his friends, his siblings, his wife—my mother, divorced from him for twenty years, present but distant, performing grief in a way that felt borrowed, rehearsed. I gave a eulogy. I don't remember what I said. I remember the sound of my own voice, strange in the quiet church, and I remember thinking that he couldn't hear me, that he was beyond hearing, beyond everything, and that this was the point, the whole point, that we speak to the dead because we cannot speak to the living, because the living are too complicated, too present, too likely to answer back.

After, people came up to me. *I'm so sorry for your loss. He was a good man. You must be devastated.* I said thank you, I'm fine, I'm handling it. I wasn't devastated. I was relieved, in a way I'm ashamed to admit. Relieved that it was over, that I wouldn't have to decide whether to visit him in the nursing home, whether to call, whether to pretend to care about a man who had never pretended to care about me. Relieved that the question was answered, finally, definitively, by something outside my control.

I cried later, in the hotel room, alone. Not for him. For me. For the child I was, waiting by the phone, hoping he would call, hoping he would show up, hoping he would be different than he was. For the adult I became, still waiting, still hoping, still unable to stop.

---

I don't know what I'm doing with this. With any of it. I write these words and I don't know who they're for. Not you, exactly, though I'm aware you're reading. Not me, though I'll read them later, maybe, in the drawer with the letters. Maybe they're for the man in the coffee shop, though he'll never see them. Maybe they're for my mother, or my father, or the version of myself at seven, standing in front of that cake, believing in good things.

I think, sometimes, that we are all just writing letters we'll never send, speaking to people who can't hear us, in languages we're still learning. I think that this is what it means to be human: to be perpetually in the middle of a sentence, never quite reaching the period, the full stop, the silence that would mean we're done, we're finished, we've said everything we need to say.

I don't believe this, not really. I believe that some things get said, eventually, or close enough. I believe that love, real love, finds its way through, despite our failures, our silences, our thousand unsent letters. I believe this because I have to, because the alternative is a loneliness I can't survive.

But I also believe that we carry our unsent letters with us, that they weigh something, that they shape us in ways we don't always recognize. I believe that the drawer will keep filling, that I will keep writing, that the words will keep coming, even when I don't know what to do with them, even when they seem to go nowhere, to mean nothing.

Tonight I'll go to bed. I'll lie in the dark and listen to my neighbor's dog, or the traffic, or the silence that follows them both. I'll try to sleep. I'll probably fail, at first. I'll think about the man in the coffee shop, and my mother, and the photograph of the girl at the birthday party. I'll think about all the things I haven't said, all the letters I'll write and not send, all the love I'll carry without delivering.

And then, maybe, I'll sleep. And tomorrow I'll wake up, and make coffee, and go to work, and try to be present, try to be here, try to be the person I was in that photograph, the one who believed that good things would keep happening.

I don't know if I believe it. But I'll try. I'll keep trying. Isn't that, in the end, all any of us can do?
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical first-person meditation that uses recurring scenes and objects to connect emotional withholding with loneliness, grief, and tentative persistence.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and self-questioning, offering the reader not a confession that resolves, but a view into the effort of living alongside what remains unsaid. Its pathos comes from the gap between care and its expression: the narrator loves their mother but cannot finish the letter, seeks company in the coffee shop without wanting contact, and feels relief as well as grief after their father’s death. The unsent letters, the photograph, and the dog barking at night make private isolation tangible. The ending offers hope cautiously, as an act of trying rather than a recovered certainty.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample centers on withheld speech and the loneliness it both protects and deepens. It repeatedly returns to family—especially the mother, the absent father, and the childhood self—as well as insomnia, ordinary routines, and observing strangers. Its moral emphasis is that love can be real despite failures of expression, while silence still has weight. The final mood is unresolved but gently persistent.

## Evidence line
> The question is which incompleteness I can live with.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the repeated letter motif, consistent emotional voice, and carefully echoed closing images make this a distinctive, coherent sample rather than a generic reflection.
